Existing restore-then-segment pipelines introduce latency and prioritize pixel-level restoration over semantic discriminability, while domain adaptation methods often face representation bottlenecks and computational complexity. We introduce LiDSeg, a framework that uses reconstruction-informed guidance to improve segmentation under adverse weather. During training, a lightweight guidance encoder is jointly optimized with the segmentation branch using segmentation and auxiliary reconstruction objectives. At inference, the reconstruction decoder is discarded, while the guidance encoder is retained to extract weather-robust features. A lightweight gated fusion module integrates these features into the segmentation branch, preserving clear-weather accuracy while improving adverse-weather robustness. On Foggy Cityscapes, LiDSeg limits the clear-to-dense-fog mIoU degradation to 2.5-2.8 percentage points, reducing the baseline performance drop by more than fivefold. On the official ACDC test server, LiDSeg-PIDNet achieves 75.07% pooled all-condition mIoU, comparable to supervised HRNet-W48 at 75.0%, while remaining substantially smaller. The gains generalize zero-shot to Foggy Driving and Foggy Zurich without training on real-fog images. LiDSeg adds only 1.9-3.1M parameters across several models, with total model sizes of 5.2-39.5M parameters and no inference-time reconstruction overhead. It delivers real-time inference on the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Code: https://github.com/yobsanb/LiDSeg

papers.title: Practical Semantic Communication for General-Purpose Networks: Compression of High-Dimensional Embeddings Under Quantization
papers.authors_text: Leonardo Roque, Louis-Adrien Dufrène, Quentin Lampin, Grégoire Lefebvre, Mohamad Assaad
papers.summary: This paper introduces a practical framework for semantic communication over wireless channels, focusing on the compression of high-dimensional embeddings under quantization and channel errors. Building upon a relaxed Gaussian Information Bottleneck (GIB) model, the approach provides analytical solutions for task-relevant information preservation, even with non-Gaussian targets. The framework relaxes traditional Gaussian assumptions, enabling effective compression for discrete and complex data such as text embeddings. It derives closed-form gradients for optimizing the compression matrix and establishes bounds linking continuous representations to discrete, noisy system performance. Comprehensive experiments on text classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms task-agnostic quantization-based compression methods, maintaining high semantic fidelity at low bit budgets per embedding. The approach offers a scalable, interpretable, and resource-efficient solution for deploying semantic communication in general-purpose networks.

papers.title: Scenario-Based Risk Certificates for Multi-Property Vulnerability Discovery in Parametric MDPs
papers.authors_text: Zhiming Chi, Andrea Turrini, Yong Li, Lijun Zhang
papers.summary: Safety-critical systems such as network protocols and distributed algorithms depend on environmental parameters whose exact values are uncertain. Parametric Markov decision processes (pMDPs) model such systems by making transition probabilities symbolic functions of the parameters. For a single quantitative requirement, parametric verification asks which parameter valuations satisfy the requirement. In practice, however, engineers often monitor several safety and performance requirements at once, and one valuation may make several requirements vulnerable simultaneously. In this paper we study multi-property vulnerability discovery under requirement-wise semantics: given a pMDP and M quantitative requirements, we construct candidate regions of the parameter space that may contain violations, and study budgets for random testing under a specified parameter distribution. To solve this, we adopt a two-layered approach in which the scenario-approximation layer provides PAC guarantees on identifying conservative vulnerability regions for each requirement while the testing layer treats random parameter exploration as coverage of overlapping regions and yields a stopping certificate computed from the marginal region masses alone; a composition theorem then bounds the expected non-discovery score by the scenario approximation error plus the testing risk from the two layers. For confirmed discoveries, candidate hits are checked by model checking and budgets use independently certified discovery probabilities. Experiment evaluate these certificates using empirical surrogates and independent confidence bounds.

papers.title: When Is the Expensive Method Worth It? A Content-Driven Analysis of Classical Bayer Demosaicing
papers.authors_text: Taranum Wasu, Harsh Kashyap, HS Pannu
papers.summary: Demosaicing reconstructs a full-colour image from a single-sensor colour-filter-array (CFA) mosaic, where only one colour is measured per pixel. Classical methods make different assumptions about images, from simple averaging to directional edge-aware interpolation, and the directional methods cost markedly more compute. We ask a practical question that a per-image quality ranking does not answer: for a given image, is the expensive directional method worth its cost? Using a controlled simulate-reconstruct pipeline on 80 benchmark images from four public datasets (Kodak, McMaster, BSD100, Urban100), six classical methods, and image-content descriptors fixed before any results were seen, we show that the quality gain of the edge-aware method (Menon 2007) over the best cheap linear method is not constant. It ranges from $-6.6$ to $+6.8$ dB, and on 31% of images it is zero or negative, meaning a cheap method matches or beats the expensive one. The gain is also predictable from content: it correlates with mean image saturation at $r=-0.86$ ($p<10^{-6}$). We then build an interpretable depth-2 decision tree that recommends the best cheap method from image descriptors, beating an always-pick-the-most-common baseline by 20.0 percentage points under leave-one-image-out validation. The analysis uses no deep learning, and every step can be inspected.

papers.title: Motor Imagery Classification Using Hybrid Cross-Subject Class Mixup and Selective Attention
papers.authors_text: Jiwon Kim, Chae-Won Lee, Jong-Seok Lee
papers.summary: Motor imagery (MI) enables a brain-computer interface (BCI) to decode movement intentions without overt movement. Hybrid electroencephalography (EEG) and functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) classification combines complementary signals, but inter-subject variability and the design of information exchange between modalities affect generalization to new subjects. We propose a framework that combines Cross-Subject Class Mixup (CSCM) with Selective Attention. CSCM aims to construct new training data to make the model robust against inter-subject variability. It independently selects EEG and fNIRS donor trials from other training subjects within the anchor class and mixes each modality while preserving the original label. Selective Attention provides an effective way to simultaneously model the temporal signal characteristics and fuse the two modalities. It retains causal temporal self-attention for EEG and uses a classification token (CLS) to integrate both modalities, without fNIRS attention updates or direct cross-modal temporal-token attention. Leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) evaluation across 28 subjects on a public EEG-fNIRS dataset yields a mean balanced accuracy (BA) of 76.85% and a macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 76.58%. The proposed model achieves the highest mean performance among five reimplemented baselines. We also examine the contributions of CSCM and Selective Attention through modality-specific mixing and donor-policy comparisons, temporal-policy comparisons, interventions on direct cross-modal paths, and component ablations.

papers.title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
papers.authors_text: Marlene Busch, Marie Weiel, Kaleb Phipps, Daniel Maldonado Quinto, Max Pargmann, Robert Pitz-Paal, Markus Götz
papers.summary: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. Efficient operation requires accurate modeling of the optical path from each heliostat to the receiver and compensation for manufacturing imperfections, kinematic misalignment, and material degradation that distort the flux distribution. Conventional ray tracers predict the flux from an assumed plant model but are limited to forward simulation. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. We present artist, an open-source, FAIR4RS-compliant Python package implementing a fully differentiable digital twin of solar tower power plants. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. Built on PyTorch, artist scales to real plants through GPU acceleration, a structure-of-arrays memory layout, and nested data parallelism. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.

papers.title: MolReps: Taking SELFIES, Making SMILES, Teaching LLMs
papers.authors_text: Ken Deng, Garrett Morris
papers.summary: The same molecule can be expressed in multiple, syntactically distinct representations, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs) can recognize and relate these equivalent encodings. We introduce MolReps, a pipeline that generates 9,600 question-answer pairs across ten representations for conversion, normalization, and 2D structure recognition. Post-training on MolReps improves text-only and multimodal models, MolQwen3-4B-Instruct (MQ3-4B-I) and MolQwen3-VL-4B-Instruct (MQ3-VL-4B-I), from $4.01\%$ to $75.13\%$ and from $7.11\%$ to $73.14\%$ (InChIKey match) on the molecule-overlap test set, respectively. On the molecule-disjoint test set, post-training increased validity from $20.35\%$ to $58.12\%$ for MQ3-4B-I and from $17.19\%$ to $59.34\%$ for MQ3-VL-4B-I. However, InChIKey match remained low, decreasing from $3.86\%$ to $3.09\%$ and from $6.44\%$ to $2.29\%$, respectively. Furthermore, the resulting models achieve a relative $27.84\%$ improvement in average over their base model on MolRepBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating molecular property prediction. These results show the effectiveness of targeted post-training for enhancing molecular representation understanding and its potential to improve downstream molecular tasks.

papers.title: EDITORS Know Your Style! Editing LoRA Subspaces for Stylistic Attribution and Imitation
papers.authors_text: Zixuan Wang, Gregory Kang Ruey Lau, Xiao Tian, Jue Fan, Caroline Chaux, Bryan Kian Hsiang Low
papers.summary: Disentangling writing style from semantic content is a fundamental challenge in literary text modeling. Style-content entanglement causes models to rely on semantic content for authorship attribution (AA) tasks and memorize author-specific content for style imitation (SI) tasks. We propose EDITORS (EditingLoRA Subspaces), a diagnose-then-deflate framework that adapts pretrained large language models and prioritizes stylistic features, making it effective for both AA and SI tasks. EDITORS first trains a diagnostic LoRA adapter using style-neutral statements derived from the training corpus to identify a content-oriented subspace. It then trains the final style adapter under activation-space deflation that projects input activations away from the identified content-oriented directions. We empirically demonstrate that EDITORS is effective. On three AA benchmarks spanning literature, social media, and news, EDITORS achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, outperforming the strongest existing baseline by up to 29%. On SI, EDITORS generates stylistically faithful and diverse passages, outperforming baselines in achieving style similarity while adhering to content specifications.

papers.title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
papers.authors_text: Hanlin Tian, Sihan Zhu, Zhao Yang, Yuxiang Wang, Zhiquan Hu, Yu Mi, Hongquan Zhu, Qiufei Hu
papers.summary:
Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists.
  We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count $L_0$ with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work $R_T$, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

papers.title: Vision-Language Model-Based Phase-OTDR Event Classification
papers.authors_text: Ahmet Bestami Kose, Mehmet Sergen Catal, Muhammet Cagri Yeke, Kivilcim Yuksel, Abdurrahman Gumus
papers.summary: Phase-sensitive optical time-domain reflectometry (Phase-OTDR) enables distributed vibration sensing, but reliable event classification has traditionally relied on fully supervised models that require extensive annotated data. This study examines the adaptability of a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for Phase-OTDR event recognition through few-shot learning. Raw samples are converted into Short-Time Fourier Transform (STFT) dB-magnitude spectrogram mosaics, color-mapped and resized to RGB images, and processed by a Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) image encoder; few-shot adaptation optimizes only the Tip-Adapter-F cache keys, leaving both encoders unchanged. Under a leakage-controlled protocol (train-side support/validation pool of 512 images per class, fixed held-out test of 120 per class, no test-set access during selection, 20 distinct support-sampling trials), the selected configuration (the ViT-L-14 Vision Transformer encoder with OpenAI weights, 128 shots per class) reaches 96.81 +/- 0.42% accuracy and a macro-averaged F1 score of 96.79 +/- 0.42% on the held-out test set; a label-efficient 16-shot setting, that is, 96 labeled support images at adaptation time across the six classes, already attains 90.17 +/- 0.81%. Tip-Adapter-F clearly outperforms both zero-shot CLIP and the standard training-free Tip-Adapter, and prompt and backbone analyses show that performance is stable across Vision Transformer encoders and insensitive to prompt wording at the selected operating point. Overall, CLIP visual features carry a transferable structure that a lightweight support cache turns into a label-efficient Phase-OTDR event classifier. The code and the corresponding image dataset are made publicly available on GitHub to support further research: https://github.com/miralab-ai/vlm-phase-otdr.

papers.title: Interpretable deep concepts of organoid morphology
papers.authors_text: Lion Jasper Gleiter, Tingying Peng
papers.summary: Image-based classification of organoid morphologies can indicate drug response, viability, or successful differentiation. In recent work, learned representations outperform handcrafted features as the basis for downstream classifiers. However, their black-box nature hides the morphological cues a classifier relies on. Based on the foundation models DINOv3 (general-purpose) and ViTAMIn-O (organoid-specific), we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to learn interpretable concepts related to distinct organoid morphologies. We annotate concepts with spatial labels (organoid, organoid wall, background) and compute their dataset specificity and task relevance across five tasks. The spatial labels of DINOv3 concepts yield coarse organoid segmentations on out-of-domain datasets. Filtering concepts by spatial label in the DINOv3-SAE improves downstream AUROC for three of the five tasks. Qualitative analysis of the most relevant concepts further reveals a confounding factor introduced by our preprocessing in one task. Through such insights, interpretable concepts could help improve the reliability of classifiers and guide the future development of organoid representation models. The trained SAEs will be made available upon publication.

papers.title: Evidence Diet: When Graph Evidence Helps LLMs Rank Competing Candidates
papers.authors_text: Yuchong Hu, Zhao Zhang, Ziyao Zhao, Haoyu Wang, Jing Xiao
papers.summary: When several candidates have graph support, does it matter which candidate receives which supporter and path counts? We study how LLM rankers use collaborative evidence on Amazon Books and MovieTV. Swapping user-level evidence degrades ranking, while matched item substitutions have little effect. On fixed clean-trained checkpoints, unrelated catalog text lowers Hit@1 from 44.77% to 38.70%, with 99.9% of rankings still valid. Across all three paired seeds, the NDCG@5 difference between count and path prompts was larger after count training than after path training. Degree matching preserves target paths while giving more rivals support. Across the full degree-matched development pools, adding candidate-level graph records to history improves NDCG@5 by 2.28 points on Books and 2.54 on MovieTV. When the target and a rival both have support, path- and count-trained rankers benefit from retaining counts. On these development queries, adding counts numerically to history scores outperforms presenting them as text. For count-trained rankers, exchanging intact count pairs among supported candidates preserves support and token length, yet lowers NDCG@5 by 4.06 points on 141 Books queries and 3.26 on 104 MovieTV queries. A frozen evaluation on 274 previously unused Books users with supported targets and rivals confirms the attribution effect: correct assignment improves pairwise accuracy by 6.07 percentage points (95% CI [4.18, 8.00]).

papers.title: Hierarchical Regime-Conditioned Dynamics for Spatiotemporal Graphs
papers.authors_text: Jeremy Baffou, Pascal Frossard, Dorina Thanou
papers.summary: Forecasting the behavior of spatio-temporal systems often requires more than accurate predictions: models should uncover the dynamical modes governing future evolution. Existing temporal graph and latent dynamical models achieve strong forecasting performance, but their latent representations often entangle multiple dynamical patterns, limiting interpretability. Conversely, regime-inference methods explicitly model such modes but typically do not support generative forecasting over graph-structured systems. We introduce HERON, a self-supervised regime-aware generative framework that unifies graph-structured trajectory generation with regime identification. HERON factorizes the latent state into discrete system-level regimes, capturing global dynamical modes, and continuous entity-level dynamics, yielding a modular regime interface compatible with existing spatio-temporal backbones. Crucially, the inferred regime actively conditions system dynamics, enabling regime tracking and controlled simulations under alternative dynamical modes. Without regime annotations, HERON jointly learns forecasts and regime dynamics in a self-supervised manner, recovering meaningful modes across controlled synthetic and real-world datasets while maintaining competitive forecasting performance. These results open a path toward interpretable, controllable generative modeling of spatio-temporal dynamics.

papers.title: ProcReverser: Multi-Agent Black-Box Microarchitectural Reverse Engineering for Processor Vulnerability Analysis
papers.authors_text: Guanqi Lyu, Decheng Qiu, Guangyang Zhang, Fei Zhao, Zhaojun Lu, Jiaji He, Yongqiang Lyu
papers.summary: When processor implementation details are unavailable, black-box microarchitectural reverse engineering helps security researchers identify hardware conditions related to security vulnerabilities. However, this process requires substantial manual effort to design experiments, develop test programs, and analyze results for each processor. We present ProcReverser, a multi-agent system that automates this process. ProcReverser uses execution feedback to improve experimental plans and test programs and identifies microarchitectural properties from measurements. We develop a comprehensive suite of property identification tasks focused on hardware mechanisms relevant to Spectre-class attacks, covering speculative execution, branch prediction, memory dependence, and cache behavior. We evaluate ProcReverser on the XuanTie C910, the gem5 RISC-V O3 CPU model, and the SiFive P550. ProcReverser achieves Pass@1 and Pass@5 scores of 81.3% and 93.8%, respectively, on C910, and 83.0% and 100.0% on gem5 O3. On the SiFive P550, ProcReverser further characterizes microarchitectural properties covered by the proposed task suite. These findings highlight the potential of automated microarchitectural reverse engineering to support processor vulnerability analysis and defense evaluation.

papers.title: Conversing with a Conversational Agent: A Real Conversation, Not a Simulated One
papers.authors_text: Christophe Denis
papers.summary: The claim that interactions with artificial conversational agents merely simulate human conversation rests on a philosophical distinction between reproducing the observable features of an activity and actually performing it. Although this distinction is appropriate for certain physical phenomena, its application to linguistic and symbolic activities is far less straightforward. This article argues that conversations with large language model (LLM)-based agents are genuine conversational activities rather than mere simulations, without thereby attributing consciousness, subjective understanding, or human intentionality to artificial systems. Drawing on the distinction between subjective and objective simulation, the article first examines the limitations of defining conversation exclusively through the intrinsic properties of its participants. It then develops a relational and semiotic account of conversational activity, informed by linguistic pragmatics, Lacan's Conversing with a Conversational Agent theory of the mirror, Baudrillard's concept of the simulacrum, Simondon's philosophy of individuation, and Peirce's semiotics. These perspectives make it possible to distinguish the reality of conversational interaction from the appearance of artificial subjectivity and from the epistemic validity of the meanings produced. The argument culminates in the concept of Hybrid Semiotic Fabrication, which characterizes meaning-making as a distributed process involving human participants, artificial intelligence, corpora, and technical arrangements. Recognizing the reality of human-AI conversation therefore entails neither anthropomorphizing artificial agents nor granting their outputs epistemic authority. Rather, it requires a more precise account of the relational, semiotic, and normative conditions under which conversational meaning is produced and justified.

papers.title: Surprise-Gated Memory for Live Speaker Diarization
papers.authors_text: Louis Mouchon, Alexis Lainault
papers.summary: We transpose the Surprise-Gated Memory recipe, a frozen encoder plus a calibrated novelty signal that gates a one-shot episodic store consolidated by periodic replay, from continual visual learning to live speaker diarization. The moment-to-moment question a streaming diarizer must answer, whether an arriving voice belongs to an already-heard speaker or a new one, is a known-versus-novel decision, exactly the decision the surprise gate is built for. On a frozen fine-tuned DiariZen backbone, our online system SGM-Diar recovers 4.8 of the 9.2 diarization-error points separating a naive online baseline from the offline oracle on AMI-SDM (52%) and 1.9 of 2.3 points on VoxConverse (82%), in the end-of-meeting revisable mode, with calibration frozen on development data and transferred cross-domain without adjustment. These are single-seed runs on three AMI meetings and five VoxConverse sessions, so the ordering of conditions rather than the absolute rates is the result. Beyond error rate, we measure the gate's behaviour directly and find a coherent memory-like profile: one-shot speaker recall at 0.857, a novelty response that habituates as speakers become familiar, re-identification that is invariant to the length of intervening silence, and a false-novelty rate of 0.001. Two ablations reproduce, now on audio, the central prediction of the visual SGM work: a sliding replay window is worse than no replay at all. The memory is strictly intra-meeting and is wiped at the end, and no gradient touches the run-time system. We report SGM-Diar as a proof-of-concept and state its limitations explicitly.

papers.title: Tight PAC-Bayes Generalisation Guarantees for Large Language Model Judges
papers.authors_text: Tom A. Lamb, Philip H. S. Torr, Tim G. J. Rudner
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) judges are increasingly used to monitor the outputs of LLM-based AI agents, yet formal guarantees on the reliability of these judges remain largely absent, limiting confidence in their use for safety-critical oversight. We consider certifying such a judge and define its risk over safety classifications of prompt--response pairs drawn from a deployed generator. We apply a PAC-Bayes framework to this setting, refining existing compression-based methodology with the use of tighter bounds and more efficient coding. We show that standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning can yield non-vacuous and even tight certificates for safety judges, for both classification and Brier risk, without holding out data for validation. We introduce LoRA-GT, which shares a single quantisation scale across layers and achieves the tightest certificates with minimal degradation in predictive performance. Across five guardrail models and four benchmarks, we find that certificate tightness is governed more by adaptation complexity than by base model scale. Finally, we show how far quantisation can be pushed before the resulting increase in risk outweighs the bound tightening gained from shorter descriptions. Together, these results provide a practical route toward certifiable scalable oversight and offer insight into how the complexity of safety adaptations shapes generalisation.

papers.title: ForeSay: Tell the Future in Words, Branch the Details in Noise for Precipitation Nowcasting
papers.authors_text: Xudong Ling, Wenjie Luo, Chaorong Li, Tianxi Huang, Tao He, Guiduo Duan
papers.summary: Precipitation nowcasting involves two distinct scales of uncertainty: macroscopic storm evolution and fine-scale local convective variations. Current generative ensemble methods entangle both scales within independent random noise draws. This coupling causes two practical limitations: every ensemble member must execute the full sampling trajectory from scratch, so an N-member ensemble costs N times a single forecast; moreover, divergent trajectories spatially misalign heavy-rain echoes across members, causing standard pixel-wise averaging to blur critical high-intensity extremes. We present ForeSay, a generative nowcasting framework that decouples macroscopic evolution prediction from local stochastic detail generation. Given historical radar frames, a vision-language model first predicts a textual scenario of future storm dynamics to condition a Rectified Flow generator. Guided by this shared macroscopic prior, ensemble members share early trunk sampling steps to establish the storm trajectory and branch with fresh noise only in later steps to explore local convective details. Because members then differ mainly in local details, self-anchored support-consensus decoding replaces pixel averaging with discrete support voting to preserve sharp heavy-rain cores. Across six datasets, ForeSay achieves the best CSI at the highest precipitation thresholds, with relative improvements over the strongest baseline on each dataset ranging from over 10% to 84%. Our 8-member ensemble retains the forecasting skill and diversity of eight independently sampled runs while reducing computational cost from 8x to 5.2x that of a single forecast.

papers.title: The Cybersecurity Dataset Observatory: Which Data for AI in Cybersecurity?
papers.authors_text: Francesco Cerasuolo, Gabriele Mangiacapre, Antonio Pescapè
papers.summary: AI is increasingly used for cybersecurity tasks such as intrusion and malware detection, in enterprise, industrial, vehicular and mobile networks. Its effectiveness depends on data: models need representative network traffic, both to be trained and to be evaluated realistically. Public datasets of cybersecurity network traffic, however, are scattered across laboratory pages, repositories and aggregators, and are continuously released, corrected and withdrawn: 92 of the 234 datasets we catalog were released in 2023 or later. At this pace, surveys that list them are outdated soon after publication, since they describe the field only as it was when they were written. We present the Cybersecurity dataset observatory, a public and continuously updated catalog of cybersecurity datasets based on network traffic. New datasets are added as they are found or submitted, every record is periodically re-checked against its original source, to which it links rather than hosting the data, and every change is recorded in a public change log. This paper documents the first release: we define a traffic-centered scope and a seven-axis taxonomy, and review 234 datasets (204 original captures and 30 derivatives) across 14 domains. The review shows a field that grows quickly but unevenly, where 91 datasets distribute only processed records, a few laboratories produce a large share of the data, and UAV, wireless and V2X networks have little public evidence, while 5G has few real captures. We then relate the catalog to common uses in AI research, outline a procedure for selecting datasets, and discuss benchmark pitfalls and open gaps.

papers.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
papers.authors_text: Kathik Iyer
papers.summary: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

papers.title: An Efficient Training Paradigm for Image Restoration via Improved Fréchet Loss
papers.authors_text: Shanyuan Jie, Wu Shi, Xinqi Lin, Kainan Yan, Zian Wang, Yingxue Pang, Yan Wang, Shijie Zhao, Chao Dong
papers.summary: Diffusion-based image restoration achieves strong perceptual quality but typically relies on iterative sampling, leading to slow inference. Existing single-step methods often use diffusion distillation or adversarial training, complicating optimization. To simplify training, we propose FDIR, a framework for training single-pass generative restoration models through regression-style supervised optimization using directly computable objectives. To realize this paradigm, FDIR employs the Fréchet distance to match the feature distributions of restored and real images in frozen representation spaces, providing explicit distribution-level supervision. To better accommodate image restoration, we incorporate local patch features to capture fine-grained restoration discrepancies. Moreover, we introduce instance-adaptive statistics by combining the feature moments of each SR-HQ pair with synchronized historical statistics, allowing distribution matching to incorporate input-specific correspondence while retaining distribution-level context. FDIR optimizes only the LoRA parameters of the restoration backbone. Experiments demonstrate strong perceptual restoration quality and efficient training, suggesting a simpler paradigm for generative image restoration.

papers.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
papers.authors_text: Maxim Konca, Alexander Mehler
papers.summary: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

papers.title: Correspondence-Free Camera Pose Estimation by Matching Moments
papers.authors_text: Subhransu S. Bhattacharjee, Dylan Campbell, Rahul Shome
papers.summary: The blind perspective-$n$-point (PnP) problem is to estimate the pose of a calibrated camera from 2D and 3D point sets with unknown correspondences. We show that, for complete, noiseless observations, fourteen permutation-invariant image moments up to order four identify a fixed camera pose for almost every 3D point set containing at least twenty points. Our learning-free method, MomentPnP, matches these moments between the observed 2D points and the projected 3D points to initialize a camera pose without correspondences and refines the pose and correspondence weights using expectation--maximization. Across the test sets of three benchmarks, our method reduces median rotation error by $5$--$170\times$ relative to the best learned baseline, both with and without outliers. We recover accurate poses even with as many outliers as inliers. On dense ETH3D scans, pose accuracy improves as the point sets grow, even as individual correspondences become harder to resolve.

papers.title: Regularizing Treatment Leakage for LLM-based Uplift Estimation
papers.authors_text: Bojing Feng, Jinqiu Deng, Zihan Hong, Yuan Xue, Wenqi Xiang, Shuhan Wang, Feng Xiao, Shiwei Wang, Zijiang Liu, Shaomin Li, Yongzhi Qi
papers.summary: Uplift modeling estimates the conditional average treatment effect (CATE) and supports industrial decisions such as promotional pricing. When large language models (LLMs) encode product text, treatment-revealing content can introduce shortcuts that do not transfer to deployment. We propose \emph{LLM-based Uplift Leakage Regularization} (\textsc{LULR}), which uses a CLUB-based penalty on the causal head's trainable shared representation while keeping the LLM encoder frozen. Controlled proxy experiments show a positive ranking-score interaction and higher scores than the tested weight-decay configuration; treatment-dependent evaluation limits their interpretation to exploratory model behavior. Structured-only comparisons provide reference performance, without establishing a general advantage over tree-based estimators. On a million-record industrial pricing RCT, \textsc{LULR} improves offline $\text{lift@}0.3$ in $4/5$ seeds, although the difference is not statistically significant and estimated policy values are near-tied. A separate one-week online A/B experiment records $5.45\%$ higher sales volume and $1.91\%$ higher GMV than the control arm. These aggregate results provide short-term business evidence for the complete deployed pricing policy; they do not isolate the regularizer's contribution.

papers.title: TRR: A Thermal Interaction Engine for Robot Simulation and RGBT Data Generation
papers.authors_text: Biwen Yang, Zhe Cao, Jin Zhang, Haoyang Sun, Zonglu Hu, Jintao Zhao, Zhehao Zhang, Kaizheng Chen, Chengyi Liu, Chengyu Wei, Siyuan Wu, Ruiheng Zhang
papers.summary: A robot's actions change the thermal conditions of its next interaction: heat retained after release, carried with objects or stored beneath the surface can change a later contact's outcome despite similar current temperatures. Training trajectories must capture how these effects connect earlier actions to later observations and task outcomes. We present TRR, a \emph{Thermal Robot Renderer} that attaches spatial and depth-resolved thermal state to both contact partners, updates local heat exchange through contact, transport and separation, and generates synchronized RGB--thermal (RGBT) observations and event-local task checks on one execution clock. Controlled interventions show why retained heat, spatial transport and internal storage matter for subsequent contact outcomes. From the same state, TRR produces a paired six-task benchmark of 2,224 static--dynamic pairs, that is, 4,448 trajectories with synchronized dual-view observations, states and actions. Visible thermal history raises safe contact-site selection from 75.0\% to 91.7\% on a dedicated learning corpus, and training on dynamic histories raises simulated transfer completion by 50 percentage points under a new heating procedure with shared feedback execution. We demonstrate RGBT observation adapters on MuJoCo and Isaac Sim, report an engineering inventory of ten prepared robot configurations and six demonstrated camera viewpoints, and describe a developer workflow that carries an existing robot scene to exported RGBT records. The benchmark, the workflow and the platform resources described in Section 6 form the first items of a planned public release. Demonstrations and resource updates are available on the project page.

papers.title: QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics
papers.authors_text: Markus Peschl, Dana Kianfar, Daniel Dijkman
papers.summary: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.

papers.title: VA-Assembly: View-Aligned Score Guidance for Training-Free 3D Part Assembly
papers.authors_text: Yeon-Jae Kim, Sangwon Kang, Byung-Kwon Min
papers.summary: Image-to-3D foundation models have improved 3D reconstruction, but typically produce monolithic representations without explicit part-level structure. Part-aware generation and learning-based assembly methods often require part-level supervision, category-specific priors, or paired part-layout training data. We instead consider a practical but underexplored setting in which independently prepared or generated 3D parts have no predefined inter-part relationships, shared coordinate frames, or consistent scales, and must be assembled into a reference-consistent object from a single image. We present VA-Assembly, a training-free framework for 3D part assembly through part-level transformation estimation using view-aligned diffusion guidance. Given a reference image and fixed 3D part geometries, VA-Assembly optimizes each part's translation, rotation, and scale. We condition a frozen view-conditioned diffusion model on same-view renderings of a reference-derived monolithic 3D representation, producing score gradients geometrically aligned with the part configuration. This guidance provides multi-view structural cues under large initial misalignment. By repurposing pretrained visual-structural priors as transformation-level supervision, VA-Assembly requires no annotated part layouts, predefined part taxonomies, category-specific assembly training, or bounding-box-based layout initialization. Experiments compare VA-Assembly with geometric registration and compositional layout baselines using each baseline's supported transformation components, showing improved part-wise transformation estimation. Ablation studies show that view-aligned conditioning, rather than diffusion guidance alone, is critical for reliable transformation gradients. Updating only part transformations preserves explicit component separability and supports component-level editing, replacement, and reconfiguration.

papers.title: PhaseCLIP: Phase-Aware Frequency-Domain Adaptation of Vision-Language Models for Few-Shot Remote-Sensing Classification
papers.authors_text: Mehmet Sergen Catal, Abdurrahman Gumus, Mehmet Zübeyir Ünlü
papers.summary: Remote-sensing (RS) image scene classification aims to assign a semantic category to an overhead image, and in practice must often do so from only a handful of labelled examples, since annotation requires expert interpretation and the resulting labels transfer poorly across sensors and regions. Recent progress has come from adapting vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP, through learned prompts or feature adapters. Although effective, these methods construct their representation entirely in the spatial domain. RS scenes are dominated by periodic texture and regular geometry, which the Fourier spectrum describes compactly through an amplitude component, carrying texture and contrast statistics, and a phase component, carrying spatial structure. Existing frequency-domain adaptation of VLMs either exploits amplitude alone or does not separate amplitude from phase, leaving the structural component unused. In this article, we propose PhaseCLIP, which inserts phase-capable spectral modules and a feature-gating module into a frozen CLIP visual encoder and trains only 1.30% of its parameters. Because the amplitude and phase pathways share an identical parameter layout, a single weight set is learned on phase and transferred exactly to amplitude, giving a two-stage scheme that adds no parameters. Experiments on five public RS datasets, EuroSAT, PatternNet, UC Merced, LSRS and RSSCN7, against eight baselines under a matched protocol, show that PhaseCLIP attains 84.28% mean accuracy and is the best method in 23 of 30 dataset-by-shot cells, with phase contributing 1.93 points overall and 4.36 points on the most difficult dataset. Because the modules act on the spectrum of image patches and transformer tokens and leave the text encoder untouched, the approach can be extended to other RS sensors and tasks, and to other domains in which class evidence lies in spatial structure.

papers.title: ThermoSight: From Appearance to Internal Thermofluid Fields via Physics-Guided Neural Reconstruction
papers.authors_text: Yuhao Fang, Chenglin Lu, Hefei Ling, Chun Lou
papers.summary: Most neural reconstruction methods focus on reproducing scene appearance, yet inferring physical states from visual observations is essential for machine understanding of the physical world. Reconstructing the internal temperature and soot fields of radiating thermofluids such as flames is challenging yet essential for improving energy efficiency and assessing heat exposure and fire spread. In flames, temperature and soot concentration jointly govern visible emission, and soot self-absorption alters the light that reaches each camera. With limited views, changes in the two fields can offset one another in the recorded RGB images, making temperature and soot difficult to disentangle. ThermoSight, a physics-guided neural framework for scientific imaging, jointly reconstructs continuous three-dimensional temperature and soot volume fraction fields from limited calibrated flame images without field-level ground truth during optimization. A differentiable spectral model links these fields to measured RGB through thermal emission, self-absorption, and calibrated camera responses. Temperature-dependent emission spectra and wavelength-dependent attenuation constrain shared fields across RGB channels, reducing temperature-soot ambiguity. Chromaticity consistency, observation-derived spatial constraints, and soot regularization complement intensity fitting. In a synthetic ablation, wavelength-resolved attenuation reduces temperature RMSE in the hot, sooty region from 234 to 112 K relative to a three-channel approximation, with nearly identical RGB PSNR (65.23 vs. 65.24 dB). Measured data yield coherent fields and competitive RGB reconstructions. These results demonstrate that physics-guided neural fields recover interpretable internal physical quantities beyond visually consistent appearance.

papers.title: EEGProbe: Do Vision-Language Models Really Understand EEG? A Benchmark for Signal-Grounded EEG Signals Evaluation
papers.authors_text: Haozhe Zhu, Dan Yuan, Chenghao Gu, Feike Xu, Yue Wen, Shin'ichi Konomi
papers.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have shown strong multimodal capabilities across scientific and biomedical domains, yet their ability to understand electroencephalography (EEG) signals remains unclear. We introduce EEGProbe, a signal-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether general-purpose VLMs can extract and reason from minimally processed, channel-wise EEG without task-specific feature engineering or EEG-specific adaptation. EEGProbe contains 620 EEG-centered questions across 13 subtasks and three capability categories: EEG Signal Classification, EEG Cross-modal Alignment, and EEG Neurophysiological Reasoning. To reduce shortcut-based answering, EEGProbe preserves the temporal structure of the recordings where possible, minimizes benchmark-induced processing, and applies signal-necessity testing followed by expert verification. We evaluate 11 representative open- and closed-source VLMs under a unified zero-shot protocol. The strongest model, GPT-5.6 Sol, achieves an overall score of only 41.63\%, with cross-modal EEG alignment emerging as a major bottleneck. We further examine model behavior from a neurophysiological perspective and analyze how temporal, spectral, spatial, and physiological EEG structure relates to model successes and failures. Inference-time neurophysiological guidance can reshape model predictions by helping models recognize the neurophysiological patterns present in the input and connect them with relevant neurological knowledge, narrowing the gap between general multimodal competence and EEG understanding. EEGProbe provides a testbed for current VLMs and a basis for developing future multimodal models that can interpret EEG evidence more reliably. The EEGProbe benchmark will be publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/2122ZHU/EEGProbe.

papers.title: Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB: An Open and Efficient Small Language Model for Fast Conversational Agents
papers.authors_text: NVIDIA, :, Adi Margolin, Aditya Malte, Aishwarya Chhabra, Alex Hodson, Ameya Sunil Mahabaleshwarkar, Ambrish Dantrey, Amy Shen, Andrii Skliar, Annamalai Chockalingam, Anusha Pant, Ashwath Aithal, Ashwin Kumar, Besmira Nushi, Bhavesh Pawar, Bryan Catanzaro, Bryan Yu, Chantal Hwang, Chenhan Yu, Chris Alexiuk, Conner Currie, Cynthia Gao, David Mosallanezhad, Dina Yared, Ehsan Hosseini Asl, Eileen Long, Erick Galinkin, Felix Friedmann, Giedrius Burachas, Gorkem Batmaz, Grzegorz Chlebus, Guillermo Siman, Haifeng Qian, Hao Guo, Hayley Ross, Hrishith Thadicherla, Hui Wang, Huiying Li, Ike Nnoli, Irina Filatova, Iris Liu, Ji-Eun Lee, Jian Leong, Jian Zhang, Jiaqi Zeng, Joey Conway, Jonathan Cohen, Jose Vergara, Julien Veron Vialard, Kari Briski, Katherine Luna, Kedar Pandurang Potdar, Kevin Ning, Khalil Ben Khaled, Krzysztof Pawelec, Laura Dykes, Leili Tavabi, Lily Lee, Linda Liu, Liwei Ding, Maka Dong, Manoj Kilaru, Maria Bagdasarova, Matthew Lee, Meredith Price, Micah Schaffer, Michael Boone, Michael Fukuyama, Michael Hasper, Nancy Agarwal, Negar Habibi, Oleksii Kuchaiev, Oluwatobi Olabiyi, Pablo Ribalta, Payal Motwani, Pinky Xu, Prasoon Varshney, Pritam Biswas, Puhui Meng, Rameshwar Shivbhakta, Ran Zilberstein, Reka Kovacs, Richard Mazzarese, Rishabh Garg, Rita Fernandes Neves, Rochelle Woods, Ruby Ye, Ruvaid Virk, Ryan Hill, Saeid Motiian, Seph Mard, Shai Ben Nun, Shaona Ghosh, Sharad Yadav, Sudeep Sabnis, Suhas Hariharapura Sheshadri, Terry Kong, Thanh Do, Thinh Le, Udi Karpas, Viet Anh Trinh, Vinay Raman, Vinita Sharma, Warren Drones, Wenwen Gao, Whei Hsueh, Will Efstratis, Yoshi Suhara, Yunsheng Liu, Zhenming Wang, Zijia Chen, Zuhair Ahmed
papers.summary: We introduce Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB, an open and efficient small language model further post-trained from Gemma-4-E4B-it and optimized for speed and intelligence per GB of memory used for fast conversational agents. The model carries forward Gemma's strong conversational capabilities and further improves multi-turn tool use, instruction following, and input grounding for fast, local voice/device assistants, interactive personas, and embedded/Edge interfaces. The model combines natural conversation with multi-turn agentic capabilities to power voice/device assistants, interactive characters and robotic/IoT interfaces running on GeForce RTX, Jetson, and RTX/DGX Spark. Experiments on 21 benchmarks show that Nemotron 3.5 Bolt E4B 4GB achieves the highest average accuracy while generating the fewest output tokens in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes, compared with Gemma-4-E4B-it and Qwen3.5-4B. The model is released with a DFlash drafter. With DFlash, Bolt E4B achieves $2.74\times$ the per-user decode speed of inference without speculative decoding at concurrency~1, and $1.21\times$ the generation throughput of Gemma-4-E4B-it with MTP at batch size 1.

papers.title: Non-Imaging Optical Tactile Sensors for Robotics: Transduction Principles, System Integration, and Robotic Applications
papers.authors_text: Hao Wu, Yu Feng, Haotian Guo, Huichan Zhao, Changsheng Wu, Jianshu Zhou
papers.summary: Non-imaging optical tactile sensors encode contact through changes in optical intensity, wavelength, spectra, or photon counts, offering diverse architectures for robotic touch. Their usefulness depends on whether contact variables can be reliably distinguished from coupled mechanical and environmental effects, and whether the resulting information can be delivered in time to guide action. This review develops a unified framework linking mechanical load transmission, optical encoding, readout, and tactile inference to robotic task requirements. It examines reflective and waveguide-based devices, micro/nanofibers, fiber gratings, interferometric and resonant structures, and mechanoluminescent composites. Three considerations emerge across these approaches. First, high optical sensitivity supports accurate tactile estimation only when target variables remain identifiable under the relevant contact and calibration conditions. Second, spatial coverage and feedback timing must be assessed at the system level, accounting for multiplexing, acquisition, demodulation, and inference. Third, device characterization, offline recognition, and closed-loop robotic performance provide distinct levels of evidence and require different evaluation criteria. Representative studies illustrate how these considerations shape force estimation, contact localization, slip correction and distributed interaction. This review concludes with priorities for calibration transfer, reliable interfaces, scalable readout, and task-based validation, providing a basis for selecting and developing non-imaging optical tactile architectures for robotics.

papers.title: Deep Learning for Satellite-Based Mountain Hazard Screening: A Retrospective Failure Analysis on the 2021 Chamoli Rock-Ice Avalanche
papers.authors_text: Snigdhajyoti Rakshit
papers.summary: The approach utilizes 10 bands from Sentinel-2 imagery, along with terrain information, in a deep learning pipeline to classify potential hazard sources in any given mountainous region. The performance of our model has been evaluated against the data collected during the rock-ice avalanche event in the Chamoli region in the Indian Himalayas on 7th February 2021. U-Net performs segmentation of the detected land surface in the satellite image, detects changes in the identify candidate hazard zones, and then the following steps are performed to calculate the potential energy using the Monte Carlo sampling for steepest descent (D8) flow paths, finding the exposed structures in the downstream locations, and ranking the zones depending on the risk score. In comparison to the simple spectral rule, our approach achieved the higher macro F1 score of 0.648 (as compared to 0.519). But the F1 score in case of rock and soil was low, being in the range of 0.3s. In case of optical change detection in winter, it's only that northeast-facing slope which couldn't be detected, as it was under 73% of shade prior to the incident. The parameters have been set for this particular scene alone and not independently; hence, this is a retrospective test, and this test locates a failure which has occurred earlier. The primary contribution of this paper is locating the pipeline leak.

papers.title: UNITE: Consolidating Embodied VLM Specialists via Shared-Anchor One-Bit Factorization
papers.authors_text: Tao Tao, Anke Tang, Enneng Yang, Zhi Hou, Xiaogang Wang, Dacheng Tao
papers.summary: Embodied capabilities such as visual grounding, spatial reasoning, navigation, and driving understanding are often developed in separate vision-language specialists fine-tuned from a common pretrained model.Deploying the specialists separately multiplies storage, whereas merging them into one dense model forces conflicting task updates to share parameters and loses part of each specialist's expertise.We introduce UNITE, a framework that consolidates such specialists into a compact shared-backbone mixture of experts. UNITE keeps the feed-forward block of each specialist as a routable expert and represents the expert bank through a shared-anchor one-bit factorization: a shared floating-point anchor plus expert-specific, row-scaled binary deviations.The anchor is optimized jointly with the scales and signs through closed-form alternating updates, using only source weights and no calibration data.Router adaptation then adjusts token-level expert selection with the backbone and experts frozen, updating fewer than $0.6$M parameters ($<0.01\%$ of the $8.8$B active parameters). Built from four Qwen3-VL-8B specialists, the complete UNITE model occupies $20.3$ GB, $1.16\times$ the storage of one dense specialist and $59.6\%$ below the uncompressed MoE. Across $22$ benchmarks and R2R Val-Unseen, UNITE matches six static merging methods in mean retention of best-specialist performance, leads all of them on Scan2Cap, ScanQA, and all four navigation metrics, and surpasses every source specialist on all five 3D scene understanding benchmarks (up to $+19.1$ on Scan2Cap) and on R2R navigation. Relative to the uncompressed MoE, factorization is nearly lossless on $21$ of $22$ benchmarks; the exception is VSI-Bench, where frame-count experiments suggest impaired use of cross-frame evidence.UNITE thus consolidates complementary embodied capabilities near single-model storage.

papers.title: STA: A Split Temporal Adversary Method for Evaluating Robustness of Multimodal RL-based Driving Policies
papers.authors_text: Shenghao Xiong, Xiaolin Chang
papers.summary: Multimodal reinforcement learning (MRL) offers a promising paradigm for autonomous driving by jointly leveraging complementary sensor observations to learn effective decision-making policies. However, its effectiveness critically depends on temporal alignment across modalities, making temporal inconsistency a fundamental vulnerability. Even subtle misalignment or latency can corrupt fused representations and ultimately lead to decision failures. Existing studies have explored adversarial attacks to induce cross-modal temporal inconsistencies, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of the temporal robustness of MRL policies. However, existing methods remain limited in generality, realism, and adaptivity. To address these limitations, we propose the Split Temporal Adversary (STA), which formulates multimodal temporal attacks as a unified decision process that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection under realistic policy-aware and budget-constrained settings. STA includes two mechanisms: a) a unified multimodal temporal perturbation mechanism that delays observations via historical states, removing the need for modality-specific noise; b) a split multimodal adversarial decision mechanism that jointly optimizes attack timing and modality selection through adaptive optimization while leveraging the victim policy's clean actions to identify sensitive decision patterns. We provide a theoretical analysis of the induced distribution shift and a modality selection principle. Experiments in the CARLA simulator show that STA more than doubles the collision rate of the strongest baseline against PPO while using 17.8\% fewer attack attempts, and that it generalizes to a VLM-based driving policy. These results reveal temporal consistency as a critical vulnerability, highlighting temporal robustness as essential for safe autonomous driving.

papers.title: Who Benefits from Telemonitoring? Uplift Modelling of a Nationwide Home Blood Pressure Monitoring Programme
papers.authors_text: Connie Kou
papers.summary: Home blood pressure (BP) telemonitoring programmes are being deployed at national scale, yet enrolment resources are finite and the benefit of telemonitoring is unlikely to be uniform across patients. We study the Primary Technology-Enhanced Care for Hypertension (PTEC-HT) programme, a nationwide telemonitoring programme for hypertensive patients in Singapore. Using retrospective data on 16,694 patients registered between August 2020 and May 2024, we first estimate the average treatment effect of the programme on 6-month BP control against a propensity-score-matched non-participant cohort, finding an absolute improvement of 5 percentage points in the rate of BP control (74% vs. 69%, $p = 3\times10^{-12}$), rising to 12 percentage points (63% vs. 50%, $p = 1\times10^{-15}$) among patients with uncontrolled BP at baseline. We then move beyond the average effect and apply uplift modelling to estimate individual treatment effects. Across five uplift learners evaluated with 5-fold cross-validation and Qini curves, an uplift random forest performed best on the full cohort and an S-learner on the uncontrolled-baseline subcohort, although performance bands overlapped across learners. On held-out patients, realised uplift was largest in the top predicted-uplift groups and declined across the ranking. These patients had higher baseline BP grade, more recent hypertension diagnosis and lower medication and diagnosis burden, a profile we offer as hypothesis-generating for targeted enrolment. A handcrafted rule built from these features was competitive with the learned models, outperforming all of them on the uncontrolled-baseline cohort, suggesting that uplift models are useful for discovering heterogeneity that can be distilled into simple enrolment criteria for directing limited care team capacity.

papers.title: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
papers.authors_text: Zhixiang Guo, Xinming Wu, Yimin Dou, Hui Gao, Siyao Zhao, He Huang, Wei Liu
papers.summary: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

papers.title: Robotic Reward Models in the Foundation-Model Era
papers.authors_text: Guoqiang Liang, Yiqi Lin, Shangchen Zhou, Wenzheng Zeng, Yanzhe Chen, Zechen Bai, Mike Zheng Shou
papers.summary: Robotic reward models (RRMs) use foundation models to replace per-task reward engineering with reusable, task-conditioned evaluation. Yet under one name, their outputs answer different questions, from whether a task succeeded to which execution is better. This survey organizes 114 methods into five semantic families by the question their native outputs answer: Outcome, Absolute Progress, Relative, Temporal Value, and Hybrid. Within this taxonomy, we review how model design determines what an evaluator can judge, how raw experience becomes supervision, and how existing evaluation practice tests the result. The review exposes a gap: agreement with demonstration order and downstream policy gains do not show whether a reward tracks task fulfillment. We therefore introduce RRM-Bench-1K, 1,117 real-robot videos of closed-loop executions with task-state and camera-evidence labels, and four contrast suites that separate the credited condition from its usual cues. A unified study of 27 evaluators shows that the strongest final scores rank whole executions well enough for selection and filtering. Dense credit, however, follows the progression of an execution more closely than its task state, and no evaluator signals when the decisive view is missing. How much fidelity a reward model needs therefore depends on the decision it drives. We outline directions from real-failure supervision to metrics that separate task state from chronology, and open-source RRM-Hub, a toolbox in which 14 existing RRMs can be readily applied and new evaluators tested on the same capabilities.

papers.title: CLIFT: Contrastive LiDAR Instance Features for 3D Pedestrian Tracking
papers.authors_text: German Devchich, Timur Akhtyamov, Denis Fatykhoph, Gonzalo Ferrer
papers.summary: A social robot has to keep track of the people around it over time to plan its motion, a task handled by 3D multi-object tracking. For the LiDAR modality, trackers usually sit on top of a detector and link its detections across frames with a separate motion model or re-identification network. We instead show how a 3D LiDAR detector itself can be turned into a tracker by adding an instance-level contrastive objective on its intermediate voxel features. Each embedding is read from the voxels inside a detected box, and boxes are matched across frames by cosine similarity and the Hungarian algorithm, without a motion model. The detector backbone is fine-tuned together with this objective, which learns identity-aware features while leaving detection accuracy essen- tially intact. Because the method uses only the voxel features that Li- DAR detectors already produce, it is backbone-agnostic. On the JRDB 3D tracking leaderboard our LiDAR-only tracker ranks first on HOTA (38.58) and IDF1 (37.99), 13.04 and 9.30 points above the next pub- lished method, and second on MOTA and OSPA. Code is available at https://hermak56.github.io/CLIFT/.

papers.title: GainCtrl: Predicting Remaining Gains for Efficient LLM Agent Execution
papers.authors_text: Kangwen Zhao, Jianfeng Cai, Ruopei Sun, Mingxiao Feng, Peng Zhang, Wengang Zhou, Houqiang Li
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used to power agents that interact with tools and environments to solve complex tasks. Repeated attempts improve the quality of tool-using agents, but continued execution incurs additional costs even when it is unlikely to improve the best result ultimately returned. This raises the question of when to stop an attempt to reduce execution cost while preserving task-level Best-of-N quality. To address this question, we introduce GainCtrl, a gain-based execution controller for LLMs. In GainCtrl, a lightweight CPU predictor uses interaction histories to estimate expected positive gains over retained scores, which are then used to guide stopping decisions with calibrated thresholds to limit the loss in mean Best-of-N task quality. We evaluate the controller through trajectory replay across three environments and three LLM actors. Comparisons of interpolated quality-cost Pareto frontiers show that GainCtrl generally uses fewer tokens than baselines at matched target quality. Fixed policies also achieve quality close to that of full execution while substantially reducing token consumption. The predictor runs at millisecond latency on a single CPU thread, supporting repeated monitoring without access to LLM internals.

papers.title: MemEmo: Evaluating Emotion in Memory Systems
papers.authors_text: Peng Liu, Zhen Tao, Jihao Zhao, Ding Chen, Yansong Zhang, Cuiping Li, Zhiyu Li, Hong Chen
papers.summary: Memory systems address the challenge of context loss in Large Language Models during prolonged interactions. However, as an essential tool for warm companionship and personalized services, the effectiveness of memory systems in processing affective information remains underexamined. To bridge this gap, we propose an emotion-enhanced memory evaluation benchmark to assess the performance of mainstream and state-of-the-art memory systems in integrating and harnessing emotional information. First, we design a benchmark called \textbf{MemEmo} to assess the affective reasoning and tracking capabilities of memory systems across four dimensions: emotional information extraction, emotional memory updating, emotional memory question-answering, and emotional conflict detection. Second, we construct the \textbf{H}uman-\textbf{L}ike \textbf{M}emory \textbf{E}motion (\textbf{HLME}) dataset to provide an empirical foundation for scrutinizing memory systems. Finally, We evaluate five representative memory systems on the HLME dataset, reporting 11 performance metrics across four dimensions. Experimental results reveal that aggregating scores for all tested memory systems is up to 45\%, far below 100\% scale, exposing a profound disparity between memory system and affective intelligence.

papers.title: Routing Beyond Task Categories: A Cost-Aware LAB-Bench Study
papers.authors_text: Ahmed Tariq, Leo Guinan
papers.summary: We tested whether features of biology questions or of a model's first answer can improve accuracy within an inference budget. In a LAB-Bench pilot, we compared a category router with one that adds six structural features. Neither reached the primary 80% accuracy target on development. At the 50% and 60% secondary targets, both chose Haiku for all 120 held-out questions and scored 71/120. We then froze a new comparison before collecting responses on 144 additional questions. Semantic routing scored 86/144. A policy that could defer after reading Haiku's answer scored 87/144. Both stayed within the inference budget of USD 0.678 per 1,000 queries. Against a 95% Haiku and 5% GPT mixture, the accuracy gains were 0.66 percentage points for semantic routing and 1.35 points for deferral. The paired 95% intervals were [-0.28,2.25] and [-0.14,3.47] points. A simple rule that escalated Haiku nonanswers scored 92/144 at USD 0.710 per 1,000 queries, above the budget. A retrospective nonanswer rule with a calibration-selected escalation probability gave an expected 85.63/144. At the learned deferral policy's observed inference cost, post hoc interpolation gave an expected 86.14/144. In a later development check, Astra and Gemini each scored 30/40. The best tested policy in each router family matched that score. The pair covered 33/40 in hindsight. The routers missed the 32/40 criterion, so the proposed 120-question evaluation did not start.

papers.title: Selective Sensor Acquisition for Multimodal Place Recognition
papers.authors_text: Margaux Edwards, Tobias Fischer, Michael Milford
papers.summary: Multimodal Place Recognition (PR) can improve robustness, but most systems rigidly read and process every sensor for every query, even when the primary sensor is sufficient, with implications for energy consumption, second sensor update rate, and domain-specific considerations such as passive stealth. We introduce selective, controllable sensor acquisition, where a user specifies a desired second sensor usage rate and the system acquires the additional sensor only when the primary sensor's estimated performance is sufficiently poor. An online threshold adjustment achieves the requested usage rate by adapting to recent primary sensor performance, directing additional sensing towards queries where fusion is most likely to help without calibration specific to sensor modality, PR method, or environment. The approach requires only a PR method that produces a match score and applies to both single-frame and sequence-based PR. Our system, across multiple datasets, PR descriptors, and sensor combinations, recovers 55% of the available PR performance gain while using the second sensor on only 25% of queries, and 81% while using it on 50%. We further analyse alternative acquisition decision mechanisms and usage-rate control methods, and examine performance when the second sensor is stronger than, comparable to, or weaker than the primary sensor.

papers.title: PEETS: Preference-aware Embeddings with Explicit Tree Structure for Auxiliary Product Bundling
papers.authors_text: Maolei Huang, Jing Tian, Dexuan Duan, Yan Chen, Huawei Cao, Shuhan Song
papers.summary: Auxiliary products such as flight protection and flexible-change services are recommended alongside primary travel purchases. This setting creates a granularity ambiguity: SKUs within one product type share semantics but differ in price and coverage, while rejecting one offer does not imply disinterest in the entire type. We present \textbf{PEETS} (\textbf{P}reference-aware \textbf{E}mbeddings with \textbf{E}xplicit \textbf{T}ree \textbf{S}tructure), a training-time framework for auxiliary product bundling. PEETS regularizes an existing click--conversion predictor through two conditional comparisons. Hierarchical Contrastive Loss uses the pair's common ancestor as a reference; Negative Contrastive Loss conditions structural sampling and comparison shifts on logged rejection events. Both act on shared SKU representations during training. This separates catalog relatedness from individual preference supervision and leaves the predictive serving path intact. PEETS achieves 78.20\% AUC, exceeding TWIN V2 by 0.90 percentage points and the matched base model by 1.15 points. In a 14-day online evaluation, gross auxiliary GMV per exposed user-day improves by 8.20\% over Policies, 3.06\% over Base, and 0.84\% over TWIN V2, with all three user-bootstrap 95\% intervals above zero. Bundling rate is 0.51 points below Policies. The cancellation interval's upper limit exceeds the prespecified margin. PEETS adds no auxiliary-loss computation to serving and records 42.1~ms p95 latency, compared with 42.0~ms for Base.

papers.title: AVD: A Multi-Sensor Teleoperated Wheelchair Platform with Safety-Aware Control
papers.authors_text: Namai Chandra, Madhur Thareja, Boby George
papers.summary: Electric wheelchairs predominantly rely on manual joystick interfaces, which present critical barriers to independent mobility for individuals with severe motor and visual impairments. This paper presents AVD (Autonomous Vehicle Drive), a dependable teleoperation architecture for assistive mobility that unifies perception, communication, embedded control, and remote supervision in a single low-cost platform built entirely from commercially available hardware. The central engineering contribution is a safety-oriented design framework: control authority follows a static hierarchy, a manual emergency stop and the occupant's joystick pre-empt remote commands, and the on-board sensing layer has stop-only authority. The compute design partitions primary and safety functions and specifies a heartbeat-driven safe-state transition for the fault cases considered. The sensing stack this framework depends on is characterized against measured data: per-channel acquisition latency, a 2,025-scan LiDAR degradation campaign spanning five target configurations and a control under water mist, airborne dust, and direct aperture occlusion, and attitude measurements across static inclines to 47 degrees. The lowest pooled environmental-condition mean retained 76.6% of the clear-baseline forward-sector yield, and no scan lost the sector completely. A logged vibration-induced inertial dropout occurred while LiDAR and camera logging continued, illustrating complementary channel behavior. The result is a documented prototype and an explicit validation path for a deployable wheelchair implementation.

papers.title: ACiT: Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers
papers.authors_text: Haixiang Wu, Zhihao Guan, Yang Yang
papers.summary: Visuomotor policies condition action prediction on visual and proprioceptive observations. While historical proprioceptive sequences carry rich dynamic priors, current methods treat them as equal to high-dimensional vision, causing the proprioceptive signal to be overwhelmed. To identify what is lost in equal-conditioning fusion, we analyze proprioceptive data and find that strong inter-joint coupling is the key action-determining structure. This finding aligns with the neural sensorimotor loop, in which proprioception first forms a body-centered prior and vision is later calibrated via parietal remapping. Inspired by this, we propose ACiT, Proprioceptive-Prior Action Chunking with Inverted Transformers, which reinforces historical joint-coupling as the primary condition with vision as a later calibration. This design is instantiated through three modules: Inverted State Encoding builds a proprioceptive prior via per-joint tokens and inter-joint self-attention. State-Visual Grounding lets joint tokens query visual evidence, making vision goal- and calibration-only. Inverted Action Chunking decodes per-joint trajectories independently. ACiT improves success rates on most LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world tasks, with the largest gains on those that require dynamics and coordination. The same conditioning design transferred to the VLA backbone pi_0-ACiT yields significant gains with better execution efficiency.

papers.title: TaF-Foundation: Wrench-Grounded Cross-Sensor Tactile Representations
